criteria.quote: Kingler’s 10,000-horsepower claw can barely be aimed.
criteria.revision: Replace the opening with: “Kingler’s claw has 10,000-horsepower strength—but it can hardly lift it.” This creates a sharper contradiction using the research’s exact claim.

criteria.quote: It can hardly lift the massive pincer, and its size makes aiming difficult.
How can Kingler’s strongest weapon also hold it back?
criteria.revision: Delay the explanation by opening with: “Kingler’s claw has 10,000-horsepower strength. So why can it hardly lift it?” Then answer that question through the later scenes.

criteria.quote: The power is real, but the pincer’s huge size makes it unwieldy.
criteria.revision: Reduce the repeated early power-and-size beats and escalate in this order: “It can hardly lift the pincer” → “Its size makes it difficult to aim” → “If it lifts it too fast, it loses balance and staggers” → “When it’s not in battle, the claw gets in the way.”

criteria.quote: Lift it too fast, and Kingler loses balance and staggers.
criteria.revision: Make this the delayed reveal and frame it as a deeper problem: “The problem isn’t only aiming. If Kingler lifts the claw too fast, it loses its balance and staggers.”

criteria.quote: Kingler’s 10,000-horsepower claw can barely be aimed.
criteria.revision: Rewrite the second scene, which repeats the first, around a new documented detail: “That oversized claw also becomes a burden outside battle—it just gets in the way.” Keep aiming, lifting, balance, and outside-battle interference as separate beats.

criteria.quote: Kingler’s claw turns strength into a trade: force first, control second.
criteria.revision: Replace the ending with: “The 10,000-horsepower claw is powerful—but Kingler can hardly lift it, struggles to aim it, and can stagger when it moves too fast.” This resolves the opening with the full cost of the strength.

criteria.quote: Which matters more: crushing power or easy aim?
